extracted.intended_audience: students and critics of the novel; novelists interested in literary craft and critical analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and critical vocabulary for judging novels according to their prophetic quality (voice that 'reaches back', extension of character, songlike voice) and their formal pattern/rhythm (shape, unity, pattern arising from plot). Useful for literary criticism or craft-focused analysis of novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophet vs preacher distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic distinguishes two modes of novelist: 'the first writer is a preacher, and the second — a prophet.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the author's focus remains on moralising or commentary (preacher) or whether characters and situations 'stand for more than themselves' and summon universals (prophet). Example: George Eliot as preacher; Dostoevsky as prophet. Note: the prophet's work implies extension beyond the immediate situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters' capacity to extend/implicate universals
rubrics_metrics.description: In prophetic fiction 'the characters and situations always stand for more than themselves; though they remain individuals they expand to embrace it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether characters remain self-contained or whether they 'extend' to represent wider humanity—e.g., Mitya 'only becomes real through what he implies' and therefore evokes universal pity. Look for sentences that imply extension beyond the immediate scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round characters capable of extension (vs flat)
rubrics_metrics.description: A character may be round yet 'capable of extension' (able to imply or summon wider human concerns), unlike a flat character who is 'adequate' in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish ordinary roundness from prophetic extendability. A character who is convincing as an individual (Hetty) may still not invite extension; another (Mitya) may be 'disproportionate' in the text but meaningful because he implies the rest of humanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic fiction's dominant impulse (extension/implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: In prophetic work 'every sentence he writes implies this extension, and the implication is the dominant aspect of his work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing prose, note whether implication/extension pervades sentence-level writing. This is not merely thematic but a stylistic and tonal quality: sentences point beyond themselves toward unity, pity, or larger human concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility and absence of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic fiction 'demands humility and the absence of the sense of humour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate tone: does the work require the reader to suspend levity and accept a solemn, humble stance? This is a positive criterion for prophecy but may be experienced as didactic or oppressive by some readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spasmodic realism / intermittent foreground detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic novels are 'spasmodically realistic'—they can be 'patiently accurate about a trial or the appearance of a staircase' but these moments are intermittencies amid larger song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for passages of painstaking realistic detail that interrupt or punctuate larger mythic or 'song' passages. These 'dents and grooves' give roughness of surface that is later subsumed into the book's unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roughness of surface that resolves into lasting smoothness
rubrics_metrics.description: While prophetic novels 'pass under our eyes they are full of dents and grooves and lumps and spikes' but 'when they have past, the roughness is forgotten, they become as smooth as the moon.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether rough, uneven passages ultimately contribute to a transcendent or unified after-effect. The temporary irregularities are a feature, not a flaw, in prophetic fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Songlike voice (not reflective argumentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The prophet 'gives us the sensation of a song or of sound' and 'does not reflect'—the prophet's voice is song rather than analytic or hammering argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish lyrical, incantatory, or musical narrative voice from explanatory, philosophical reflection. A prophetic voice evokes rather than reasons; it sings instead of arguing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy versus fantasy distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophecy is 'face towards unity' whereas fantasy 'glances about'; prophecy's confusion is incidental, fantasy's confusion is fundamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying a work, determine whether its ambiguities serve a unilateral drive toward unity (prophecy) or are intrinsic to playful multiplicity (fantasy). This affects how one judges coherence and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underlying song/undercurrent beyond plot (example: Moby Dick)
rubrics_metrics.description: In works like Moby Dick 'the prophetic song... flows athwart the action and the surface morality like an undercurrent' and cannot be fully stated in words or reduced to simple symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the novel contains an ineffable undercurrent (a 'song') that gives depth beyond the plot. Beware reductive readings that convert elements into flat symbols—these may 'silence the book.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern as an aesthetic shape of the book
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern 'is an aesthetic aspect of the novel' that 'causes us to see the book as a whole'—the critic borrows pictorial images (hour-glass, grand chain) to describe it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the novel's overall structural shape and whether its parts (characters, incidents, plot) cohere into a recognizable pattern that enhances aesthetic pleasure. Use metaphors (hour-glass, chain) as heuristic tools to show unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern springs mainly from the plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern 'springs mainly out of the plot' and 'draws most of nourishment from the plot.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging pattern, trace how the sequence and arrangement of events produce the book's shape. The plot is the principal source of pattern, though characters and atmosphere also contribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of pattern to authorial mood/atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful pattern is one whose form is 'suitable to the author's mood' so that the pattern reinforces the book's atmosphere (example: Roman Pictures' 'grand chain' fitting its comic, sub-acid mood).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the chosen structural pattern matches the tone and atmosphere. A mismatch weakens the work; a congruent pattern strengthens aesthetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern may require authorial sacrifices
rubrics_metrics.description: An author may have to make 'sacrifices... if he wants his pattern and nothing else to triumph.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to elements the author restrains or flattens to preserve unity (e.g., avoiding extraneous detail or explanation). Decide whether such sacrifices serve the work or impoverish it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern vs rhythm distinction (when beauty is not shape)
rubrics_metrics.description: If beauty is not the overall 'shape of the book' the critic will call it 'rhythm' rather than pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between holistic structural unity (pattern) and qualities that arise from recurring motifs, pacing, or musicality (rhythm). Both are aesthetic criteria but apply to different manifestations of beauty in a novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters/incidents must elaborate and work for the pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: In a patterned novel 'none of the minor characters are just decorative... they elaborate on the main theme, they work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate minor characters and episodes for their functional contribution to the book's pattern: do they advance the central symmetry or theme, or are they merely decorative?
